passages.text: Abnormal ClC-3/TMEM9-mediated endosomal ion transport in <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic>-associated neurodevelopmental disease

Endolysosomal abnormalities are particularly detrimental to the nervous system and have been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders. <sentence_start/>Key regulators of the lysosomal and endosomal luminal ion homeostasis are CLC chloride/proton exchangers. <sentence_start/>We report 15 individuals carrying variants in <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic>, encoding a ubiquitous endosomal 2Cl<sup>−</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> exchanger, and provide updated clinical information for 5 previously reported individuals. <sentence_start/>Subjects displayed a broad spectrum of neuropsychiatric symptoms, including developmental delay, intellectual disability, and epilepsy. <sentence_start/>To reveal the pathogenic mechanism, we investigated ClC-3 variants-mediated ion transport and its regulation by the recently discovered inhibitory beta subunit TMEM9. 12/20 missense variants exhibited altered properties and fell into two classes: those affecting the region binding inhibitory TMEM9 carboxy-termini, and those that broaden the voltage range over which ClC-3 conducts ions. <sentence_start/>Surprisingly, the latter variants also attenuated TMEM9-mediated inhibition. <sentence_start/>Both classes produced a toxic gain-of-function, as evident from endolysosomal vacuolization by mutant ClC-3/TMEM9 overexpression. <sentence_start/>Our results expand the genetic and clinical spectrum of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3-</italic>related disease, provide a solid basis for genetic counseling, and uncover an unexpected link between gating-associated conformational changes and inhibition by TMEM9.
Synopsis

Loss- and gain-of-function variants of the endosomal chloride/proton exchanger ClC-3 are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders. <sentence_start/>Identification and characterization of novel variants expands the clinical spectrum of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> disease and provides detailed insights into pathogenic mechanisms.
Most heterozygous missense variants result in a gain of function when studied in co-expression with TMEM9 β-subunits.
Several variants affect ClC-3 residues close to the binding pocket of the TMEM9 carboxy-terminus that directly blocks the chloride pathway, thereby weakening the block.
Several other variants, located far from the binding site, affect voltage-dependent gating when studied without TMEM9, thereby enhancing currents at endosomal voltages.
These variants also weaken TMEM9-mediated inhibition, revealing a link between gating-associated conformational changes and TMEM9 binding.

Loss- and gain-of-function variants of the endosomal chloride/proton exchanger ClC-3 are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders. <sentence_start/>Identification and characterization of novel variants expands the clinical spectrum of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> disease and provides detailed insights into pathogenic mechanisms.
The paper explained
Problem

Luminal ion homeostasis is essential for endosome and lysosome function, including protein sorting, metabolism, and signaling. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, mutations in endolysosomal ion channels and transporters cause various inherited diseases, often with prominent neurological manifestations because neurons depend on precise intracellular trafficking and cannot dilute toxic material through cell division.

Five chloride/proton exchangers of the <italic toggle="yes">CLCN</italic> family regulate pH and chloride concentrations in overlapping endolysosomal compartments, and mutations in all of them are linked to disease. <sentence_start/>Loss of the late-endosomal ClC-3 transporter (encoded by <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic>) causes severe neurodegeneration, while several human variants have been associated with neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders. <sentence_start/>However, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unclear, particularly because previous studies did not account for the recently identified obligatory β-subunits TMEM9A and TMEM9B, which regulate the trafficking and transport activity of ClC-3, ClC-4, and ClC-5.
Results

We expanded the clinical and genetic spectrum of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> disease by identifying 15 additional patients with neurodevelopmental disorders and characterizing these and previously unstudied variants using electrophysiological and cell-biological approaches. <sentence_start/>Most variants were heterozygous, occurred de novo, and affected residues distributed throughout the protein. <sentence_start/>Developmental delay typically becomes apparent during infancy, with symptoms appearing at an average age of seven months. <sentence_start/>Common features included impaired speech development, ataxia, autistic traits, and epilepsy.

Functional analyses incorporating TMEM9 co-expression showed that most disease-causing variants confer a gain of function by weakening TMEM9-mediated inhibition. <sentence_start/>This likely enhances H<sup>+</sup>-driven Cl<sup>−</sup> accumulation, causing osmotic swelling and the formation of enlarged lysosome-like vacuoles. <sentence_start/>Several variants affected residues within the PI(3,5)P<sub>2</sub>-binding pocket that stabilizes the interaction between TMEM9 and ClC-3. <sentence_start/>However, other variants reduced TMEM9-mediated inhibition despite being located far from this interface. <sentence_start/>These variants altered ClC-3 voltage-dependent gating even in the absence of TMEM9.
Impact

Our study shows that heterozygous <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants cause a toxic gain of function by reducing inhibition of the late-endosomal Cl<sup>−</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> exchanger ClC-3 by TMEM9 β-subunits, resulting in a broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.

Importantly, reduced TMEM9-mediated inhibition is not limited to variants near the TMEM9/PI(3,5)P<sub>2</sub> interface but also occurs with variants that alter ClC-3 gating. <sentence_start/>This suggests that gating-associated conformational changes influence the binding of TMEM9 and/or PI(3,5)P<sub>2</sub>.

These findings identify the ClC-3/TMEM9 complex as a potential therapeutic target. <sentence_start/>Although pharmacological inhibition of ClC-3 may benefit patients with ClC-3 hyperactivity, specific inhibitors are not yet available and would likely need to be administered early in disease progression.
Introduction

The survival and function of cells critically depend on the endolysosomal system, which plays a key role in the uptake and processing of extracellular substances, trafficking of membrane proteins, degradation of intracellular organelles, metabolic signaling, and many other processes. <sentence_start/>Impaired endolysosomal function is particularly deleterious for the nervous system because adult neurons cannot dilute protein aggregates through cell division and depend on precise subcellular trafficking to maintain the highly specialized localization of essential proteins. <sentence_start/>For instance, lysosomal storage diseases, although affecting lysosomes throughout the body, often manifest with prominent neurological signs.

Ion transporters along the endocytic pathway maintain the appropriate environment for the activity of luminal enzymes and affect vesicle trafficking and maturation (Chadwick et al, <citation rid="CR4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ceb.2021.02.006" pmid="33706237" count="1">2021</citation>; Scott and Gruenberg, <citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/bies.201000108" pmid="21140470" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Vesicles in the endolysosomal pathway are progressively acidified by the vesicular H<sup>+</sup>-ATPase and reach a luminal pH of about 4.7 in lysosomes (Freeman et al, <citation rid="CR12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/physrev.00009.2022" pmid="35981302" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Vesicular 2Cl<sup>−</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> exchangers of the CLC family (Jentsch and Pusch, <citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/physrev.00047.2017" pmid="29845874" count="1">2018</citation>), ClC-3 to ClC-7, may provide a shunting conductance for vesicular acidification (Günther et al, <citation rid="CR13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s00424-002-0950-6" pmid="12548389" count="1">2003</citation>; Hara-Chikuma et al, <citation rid="CR16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M407030200" pmid="15504734" count="1">2005</citation>; Li et al, <citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/ajpcell.00504.2001" pmid="11997263" count="1">2002</citation>; Novarino et al, <citation rid="CR33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1188070" pmid="20430975" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition, these CLCs raise luminal Cl<sup>−</sup> concentration, which by itself is critical for vesicle maturation and enzyme activity (Cigić and Pain, <citation rid="CR7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1432-1327.1999.00697.x" pmid="10491143" count="1">1999</citation>; Weinert et al, <citation rid="CR51" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.1188072" pmid="20430974" count="1">2010</citation>; Scott and Gruenberg, <citation rid="CR43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/bies.201000108" pmid="21140470" count="1">2011</citation>; Chakraborty et al, <citation rid="CR5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.28862" pmid="28742019" pmcid="PMC5526669" count="1">2017</citation>; Wu et al, <citation rid="CR52" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1083/jcb.202208155" pmid="37010469" pmcid="PMC10072274" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>The biological importance of endolysosomal CLC exchangers is evident from knockout (KO) mouse models for all endolysosomal CLCs (Jentsch and Pusch, <citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/physrev.00047.2017" pmid="29845874" count="1">2018</citation>) and from more recent reports that rare genetic changes in endosomal ClC-3 (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>), ClC-4 (Veeramah et al, <citation rid="CR48" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/epi.12201" pmid="23647072" pmcid="PMC3700577" count="1">2013</citation>; Palmer et al, <citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/mp.2016.135" pmid="27550844" pmcid="PMC5794876" count="1">2018</citation>) and ClC-6 (Polovitskaya et al, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2020.11.004" pmid="33217309" pmcid="PMC7820737" count="1">2020</citation>) are associated with a spectrum of human neuropsychiatric disorders.

The CLC gene family encodes both plasma membrane Cl<sup>−</sup> channels and intracellular 2Cl<sup>−</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> exchangers (Jentsch and Pusch, <citation rid="CR20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/physrev.00047.2017" pmid="29845874" count="1">2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>CLCs function as dimers, with each subunit possessing its own permeation pathway, which can be gated independently. <sentence_start/>Coordinated, voltage-dependent activation of both subunits-referred to as common gating-requires large conformational changes that include the cytosolic carboxy-termini (Duffield et al, <citation rid="CR8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1085/jgp.20028741" pmid="12566541" pmcid="PMC2217322" count="1">2003</citation>; Ludwig et al, <citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M113.509364" pmid="23983121" pmcid="PMC3789960" count="1">2013</citation>; Wan et al, <citation rid="CR49" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-024-50975-w" pmid="39107281" pmcid="PMC11303396" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>While most CLCs function as homodimers, ClC-3 can associate with ClC-4 to form heterodimers (Suzuki et al, <citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcp.20516" pmid="16222710" count="1">2006</citation>; Guzman et al, <citation rid="CR14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M117.801951" pmid="28972156" pmcid="PMC5704486" count="1">2017</citation>; Weinert et al, <citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.2019103358" pmid="32118314" pmcid="PMC7196918" count="1">2020</citation>).

The ClC-3 exchanger is found in all tissues, including neurons, where it localizes primarily to endosomes and less so to synaptic vesicles (Stobrawa et al, <citation rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0896-6273(01)00189-1" pmid="11182090" count="1">2001</citation>; Li et al, <citation rid="CR28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1152/ajpcell.00504.2001" pmid="11997263" count="1">2002</citation>; Suzuki et al, <citation rid="CR46" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/jcp.20516" pmid="16222710" count="1">2006</citation>; Weinert et al, <citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.2019103358" pmid="32118314" pmcid="PMC7196918" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>Its localization depends on alternative splicing, which alters its cytoplasmic amino-terminus. <sentence_start/>ClC-3a and ClC-3b reside in late endosomes, whereas ClC-3c is targeted to recycling endosomes and can partially reach the plasma membrane, where it is amenable to electrophysiological analysis (Guzman et al, <citation rid="CR15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M115.668186" pmid="26342074" pmcid="PMC4646242" count="1">2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>Genetic ablation of <italic toggle="yes">Clcn3</italic> in mice caused profound neurodegeneration (Stobrawa et al, <citation rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0896-6273(01)00189-1" pmid="11182090" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>In humans, severe neurodevelopmental disorders were found in subjects carrying <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants, some of which exhibited loss or gain of transport function (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>).

Recently, the single transmembrane domain proteins TMEM9 (T9A) and TMEM9B (T9B) were identified as obligatory β-subunits of ClC-3, -4 and -5 (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>These subunits are crucial for protein stability, trafficking, and regulation of ion transport. <sentence_start/>Both subunits have similar roles as shown by functional assays and KO mice. <sentence_start/>A cytosolic phosphorylated acidic cluster (pAC) on TMEM9/9B (collectively referred to as T9) proteins reduces the plasma membrane expression of CLC/T9 complexes. <sentence_start/>Unlike other CLC β-subunits such as Ostm1 (Lange et al, <citation rid="CR24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature04535" pmid="16525474" count="1">2006</citation>), barttin (Estévez et al, <citation rid="CR10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/35107099" pmid="11734858" count="1">2001</citation>) or GlialCAM (Jeworutzki et al, <citation rid="CR21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2011.12.039" pmid="22405205" pmcid="PMC3334819" count="1">2012</citation>), T9 proteins tonically inhibit CLC ion transport, with their C-terminal inhibitory domains (CID) blocking the cytoplasmic opening of the Cl<sup>−</sup> pathway (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>; Schrecker et al, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-025-01617-2" pmcid="PMC12403049" pmid="40670814" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Partial relief of this inhibition enables a large dynamic range of activation. <sentence_start/>The discovery of these obligatory subunits required a revision of previous analysis of disease-causing variants in <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CLCN4</italic>. <sentence_start/>Several pathogenic variants located close to the T9 binding site display a toxic gain of ion transport because they partially lost their sensitivity to T9-mediated inhibition (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>).

Until now, only one homozygous and 10 heterozygous potentially disease-causing variants of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> have been reported (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>; Nakashima et al, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s10038-022-01106-0" pmid="36536096" pmcid="PMC12327483" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>Common clinical findings included moderate to severe developmental delay, intellectual disability, structural brain abnormalities, behavioral disorders, hypotonia, seizures, and failure to thrive. <sentence_start/>Functional analysis had only been performed for a subset of variants (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>) and, with two exceptions (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>), lacked co-expression of T9 subunits. <sentence_start/>The mechanisms by which these variants lead to disease remain largely unclear.

The aim of our study is to expand the genotypic and phenotypic spectrum of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic>-related neurodevelopmental disorders and to understand the biophysical and cellular mechanisms by which variants lead to pathology. <sentence_start/>We identified additional subjects carrying rare <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants, thereby expanding the known spectrum of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic>-related disorders. <sentence_start/>Functional analysis of these and previously published variants suggested that more than 65% of missense variants were hyperactive in the presence of the inhibitory T9A subunit, consistent with their pathogenicity in heterozygous subjects. <sentence_start/>Our study shows that even changes in residues not located close to the region that binds the inhibitory domain of T9A can partially relieve T9A-mediated inhibition and reveals a link between ClC-3 gating and T9-mediated inhibition.
Results
Cohort description

We newly describe 15 unrelated individuals with neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) harboring <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants. <sentence_start/>With one exception (p.Thr570Ile), these variants have not been described before. <sentence_start/>Together with the previously published group of 11 individuals carrying 10 different variants (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>), the combined cohort of 26 individuals carried a total of 20 missense (one found in three subjects), 1 in-frame deletion of a single amino acid, 1 splice-site, and 1 truncating variant (found in two siblings (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>)). <sentence_start/>With one exception (p.Trp385Cys), the missense variants were found in a heterozygous state.

We focused clinical analysis on those 16/26 subjects whose variants resulted in functional changes of ClC-3 when analyzed in vitro, or on those carrying homozygous likely loss-of-function variants. <sentence_start/>Detailed clinical and genetic information for these 16 individuals, together with a short summary of our functional analysis, is provided in Dataset EV1 and in an abridged form in Table 1. <sentence_start/>Dataset EV2 gives a short summary of clinical features, in silico predictions and functional results for variants that appear normal in our functional assays.

The 16 subjects carrying function-changing <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants (Table 1), of whom 6 had been reported previously (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>), were unrelated (7 females and 9 males). <sentence_start/>The median age at inclusion was 9 years (range 23 days to 25 years). <sentence_start/>Subject #1 carried a homozygous splice-site variant likely resulting in a loss-of-function (LOF), and subject #2 a biallelic variant predicting nonsense-mediated RNA decay and/or the production of a severely truncated, non-functional protein. <sentence_start/>One individual (#3) was homozygous for a missense variant leading to functional changes with unclear biological impact, whereas the remaining individuals carried heterozygous missense variants (or an in-frame deletion of a single amino), which led to a gain-of-function (GOF) in the functional assays described below. <sentence_start/>The heterozygous GOF variants were de novo (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 12) or of unknown inheritance (<italic toggle="yes">n</italic> = 1). <sentence_start/>The variants, including those previously described (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>; Nakashima et al, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s10038-022-01106-0" pmid="36536096" pmcid="PMC12327483" count="1">2023</citation>), affected cytoplasmic amino- and carboxy-termini, transmembrane helices and connecting loops of the encoded ClC-3 protein (Fig. 1A,B).Figure 1
Positions in the ClC-3 protein of amino acids altered in subjects with NDD.

(<bold>A</bold>) Schematic diagram of a ClC-3 monomer, depicting α-helices determined from cryo-EM structures as rectangles and cytoplasmic CBS (cystathionine β-synthase) domains as ovals. <sentence_start/>Functional characteristics of mutants coded by different symbols, with variants newly described here shown as circles. <sentence_start/>(<bold>B</bold>) Localization of these residues in the cryo-EM structure of ClC-3/T9A (PDB: 9DNX) (Schrecker et al, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-025-01617-2" pmcid="PMC12403049" pmid="40670814" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>ClC-3 subunits shown in shades of gray, and T9A in beige. <sentence_start/>Individual ClC-3 monomers of the homodimer depicted in different shades. <sentence_start/>The box shows the magnification of the interface between ClC-3 and the CID of T9A, with residues altered in NDD subjects highlighted. <sentence_start/>Phosphatidylinositol-3,5-bisphosphate (PI(3,5)P<sub>2</sub>) (shown in green) is sandwiched between ClC-3 and the carboxyterminal inhibitory domain (CID) of T9A.

In silico predictions for the pathogenicity of these variants were obtained as detailed in Methods, with results given in Datasets EV1 and EV2. <sentence_start/>The mean CADD score across heterozygous variants with detected functional changes (Table 1 and Dataset EV1) was 28.6, ranging from 23.7 to 33.0, whereas CADD scores for the missense variants without detected functional alterations (Dataset EV2), ranged from 21.1 to 28.3. <sentence_start/>Two of the latter variants, but none of those listed as likely pathogenic (Datasets EV1 and EV2), occurred once in gnomAD v4.1.0.
Clinical findings of subjects carrying variants that affect ClC-3 function

Clinical findings are summarized in Table 1 and Dataset EV1. <sentence_start/>Frequencies are reported as n/N, with N indicating the number of individuals for whom the respective feature was available. <sentence_start/>Among the 16 individuals carrying function-changing <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants or biallelic likely loss-of-function variants, the most frequent clinical hallmarks were developmental delay and/or intellectual disability (13/13, 100%), gross motor delay or impaired ambulation (13/14, 93%), intellectual disability (11/12, 92%), vision or eye abnormalities (11/13, 85%), language impairment (11/14, 79%), behavioral or psychiatric features (10/14, 71%), gastrointestinal or feeding symptoms (10/16, 63%), hypotonia (8/13, 62%), and autistic features (8/13, 62%).

Developmental concerns were recognized early, at a mean age of 6.7 months, ranging from the neonatal period to 18 months. <sentence_start/>Neonatal findings were present in 10/16 individuals (63%) and mainly included hypotonia (8/13, 62%), neonatal feeding difficulties (8/16, 50%), and failure to thrive (4/16, 25%). <sentence_start/>Where the distribution of hypotonia was specified, it involved both axial and limb musculature in 6/7 individuals and was restricted to central hypotonia in 1/7; one additional individual was reported as hypotonic without further specification.

Motor development was commonly delayed. <sentence_start/>Sitting age was reported for 9/16 individuals and ranged from 6 to 18 months. <sentence_start/>Independent walking, when achieved, occurred between 1.3 and 6 years. <sentence_start/>Two individuals walked only with support, and at least two remained non-ambulant beyond 3 years of age. <sentence_start/>Movement disorders were reported less consistently and included ataxia in 3/10 individuals (30%) and dystonia in 3/11 (27%). <sentence_start/>Additional isolated findings included extrapyramidal hypertonia with global akinesia, tics, tremor, lower-limb spasticity, and severe bilateral spastic cerebral palsy.

Cognitive and language impairment formed a central part of the phenotype. <sentence_start/>Developmental delay and/or intellectual disability were present in all individuals with available data (13/13, 100%). <sentence_start/>Intellectual disability was reported in 11/12 individuals (92%) and ranged from mild to severe among individuals aged 6 years or older. <sentence_start/>Formal neuropsychological testing was available for two individuals; in the remainder, the degree of impairment was based on clinical assessment. <sentence_start/>Language impairment was present in 11/14 individuals (79%). <sentence_start/>At last follow-up, 8/12 individuals with available information had some verbal communication, ranging from single words to fluent speech, whereas 4/12 remained non-verbal at last follow-up.

Behavioral and psychiatric manifestations were frequent (10/14, 71%). <sentence_start/>These included autistic features in 8/13 individuals (62%), self-damaging behavior in 6/13 (46%), anxiety in 6/11 (55%), ADHD in 3/10 (30%), and aggressive behavior in 2/13 (15%). <sentence_start/>Sleep disorders were reported in 7/12 individuals (58%), including severe sleep apnea in 2/12 and narcolepsy in 1/12. <sentence_start/>Developmental regression occurred in 4/12 individuals (33%) and affected language, motor function, cognition, and/or social skills. <sentence_start/>Of note, all these individuals displayed autistic features.

Epilepsy was present in 7/16 individuals (44%), with seizure onset ranging from the neonatal period to 6.5 years. <sentence_start/>Seizure type at onset was available for 5/7 individuals with epilepsy and included epileptic spasms, focal-onset hypermotor seizures, myoclonic seizures, absences, and unknown-onset seizures with impaired awareness. <sentence_start/>Two individuals developed additional seizure types during follow-up, and one experienced status epilepticus. <sentence_start/>At the last follow-up, 2/7 individuals with epilepsy were seizure-free, whereas 1/7 had treatment-resistant seizures.

Brain MRI was abnormal in most individuals for whom imaging was available. <sentence_start/>The most recurrent findings were hypoplasia or agenesis of the corpus callosum and pontine hypoplasia. <sentence_start/>Additional findings included cerebral atrophy, ventriculomegaly, abnormal white-matter signal, mild cerebellar tonsillar descent, prominent superior cerebellar peduncle, aqueductal stenosis with small vermis, enlarged perivascular spaces, and an arachnoid cyst.

Vision or eye abnormalities were reported in 11/13 individuals with available ophthalmological information (85%). <sentence_start/>Specific findings included strabismus in 7/11 individuals (64%), refractive errors in 5/13 (38%), nystagmus in 4/13 (31%), cortical visual impairment in 2/10 (20%), and retinal or optic abnormalities in 2/13 (15%). <sentence_start/>Oculomotor apraxia, pigment loss, and photophobia were each reported in one individual. <sentence_start/>Hearing loss was reported in 2/12 individuals (17%).

Gastrointestinal or feeding symptoms were present in 10/16 individuals (63%). <sentence_start/>These included neonatal feeding difficulties in 8/16 (50%), chronic constipation in 6/13 (46%), gastroesophageal reflux in 5/14 (36%), and need for a permanent feeding tube in 2/12 (17%). <sentence_start/>Pulmonary features were reported in 4/11 individuals (36%) and included recurrent infections in 3/11, asthma or reactive airways in 2/11, and severe sleep apnea in 2/11.
Functional analysis of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants

All but one variant affecting one amino acid were identified in the heterozygous state. <sentence_start/>Two of the three remaining homozygous variants affect either intronic sequences close to a splice site (#1) or lead to an early frameshift (#2, individual 10.1 reported by (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>)). <sentence_start/>These LOF variants cannot be tested functionally in our assays.

ClC-3 missense and in-frame deletion variants were characterized using electrophysiological recordings of plasma membrane currents and microscopy-based analysis of endolysosomal compartments. <sentence_start/>Both methods relied on ClC-3 overexpression in mammalian cells. <sentence_start/>Electrophysiological studies employed the ClC-3c splice variant, which partially localizes to the plasma membrane upon overexpression (Guzman et al, <citation rid="CR15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M115.668186" pmid="26342074" pmcid="PMC4646242" count="1">2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>Vacuole formation was analyzed using ClC-3a, which targets late endosomes and induces enlarged vacuoles when not inhibited by T9A. This approach enables assessment of ClC-3 function in its native endosomal context and provides a sensitive assay for the modulation of ClC-3 activity by recently identified T9 β-subunits (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>These splice variants have identical ion transport properties when directed to the plasma membrane (Guzman et al, <citation rid="CR15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M115.668186" pmid="26342074" pmcid="PMC4646242" count="1">2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, their localization to various membranes, which differ in lipid and phosphatidylinositide composition, may differentially affect their activity. <sentence_start/>In both assays, N-terminally Venus-tagged ClC-3 constructs were used to identify transfected cells. <sentence_start/>We also extended our analysis to previously described variants (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>) that lacked electrophysiological analysis or assessment of inhibition by T9 subunits.

The appearance of 2Cl<sup>−</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> exchange currents at negative potentials may represent a toxic gain of function. <sentence_start/>In vivo, however, all endosomal CLCs associate with obligatory T9 β-subunits that strongly inhibit their ion transport (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>It is therefore crucial to determine whether these additional currents escape T9-mediated inhibition. <sentence_start/>Because T9 proteins suppress ClC-3 PM currents both by blocking the Cl<sup>−</sup> pathway and by reducing surface expression (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>; Schrecker et al, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-025-01617-2" pmcid="PMC12403049" pmid="40670814" count="1">2025</citation>), we co-expressed ClC-3 variants with T9A<sup>ΔpAC</sup>, a mutant lacking an internalization signal that traffics to the surface together with the CLC protein. <sentence_start/>Indicating potent T9 inhibition, resulting currents from three variants (p.Ile607Val, p.Ile607Thr, and p.Val324Ala) were indistinguishable from background (Figs. 2E and EV1C). <sentence_start/>This was not observed with a control construct (T9A<sup>ΔpAC,ΔCID</sup>) (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>) with additional disruption of the C-terminal inhibitory domain CID (Figs. 2E and EV1C). <sentence_start/>In the vacuolization assay, which reflects cumulative ClC-3 activity overexpression time (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>), however, vacuole generation by these variants was resistant to WT T9A (Fig. 2F,G), although the altered residues cannot directly interact with T9’s CID because they are located within the transmembrane region (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>; Discussion
Both loss- and gain-of-function of ClC-3 can cause human disease

Loss-of-function (LOF) variants of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> can lead to human neurodegenerative/developmental disease, as evident from the homozygous p.Lys112Asnfs*6 variant that truncates the ClC-3 protein before the first transmembrane domain (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>). <sentence_start/>It was found in two siblings, one of whom was followed up clinically in the present study (#2). <sentence_start/>Subject #1, who harbored a homozygous splice-site variant likely also leading to LOF, now adds a similar case. <sentence_start/>In mice, KO of ClC-3 entails severe neurodegeneration, which eventually results in a loss of the hippocampus (Stobrawa et al, <citation rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0896-6273(01)00189-1" pmid="11182090" count="1">2001</citation>; Yoshikawa et al, <citation rid="CR53" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1365-2443.2002.00539.x" pmid="12059962" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>Interestingly, similarly severe neurodegeneration is observed when only one aspect of ClC-3 function, the exchange of chloride for protons, but not chloride permeation, is eliminated in <italic toggle="yes">Clcn3</italic><sup>unc/unc</sup> mice by a single point mutation-but only when studied in a <italic toggle="yes">Clcn4</italic><sup>−</sup><sup>/</sup><sup>−</sup> background (Weinert et al, <citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.2019103358" pmid="32118314" pmcid="PMC7196918" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>This is because ClC-3 and ClC-4, which in the brain mostly occur as heterodimers, can largely substitute for each other functionally (Weinert et al, <citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.2019103358" pmid="32118314" pmcid="PMC7196918" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>Notably, the trafficking and stability of ClC-4 depend on the presence of ClC-3. <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">Clcn3</italic><sup>−/−</sup> mice, levels of ClC-4 proteins are markedly decreased, further potentiating the insult caused by the lack of ClC-3 (Weinert et al, <citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.2019103358" pmid="32118314" pmcid="PMC7196918" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>We expect the same for subjects #1 and #2.

Of note, the pathology caused by the loss of ClC-3 cannot be attributed entirely to the resulting loss of ClC-4, as demonstrated by the pathology of <italic toggle="yes">Clcn3</italic><sup>td/td</sup> mice with disrupted ClC-3 ion transport, but maintained stabilization of ClC-4 (Balduin et al, <citation rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-025-19757-2" pmid="41023377" pmcid="PMC12479943" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Conversely, disruption of ClC-4, which does not affect ClC-3 levels, can lead to pathology (Palmer et al, <citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/mp.2016.135" pmid="27550844" pmcid="PMC5794876" count="1">2018</citation>), although it is milder than with ClC-3 LOF, which goes hand in hand with a loss of ClC-4. <sentence_start/>Hence, the ability of ClC-3 and ClC-4 to substitute for each other functionally is not complete.

The heterozygous parents of LOF variants carrying #1 and #2 were unaffected, agreeing with the absence of pathology in heterozygous <italic toggle="yes">Clcn3</italic><sup>+/−</sup> mice (Stobrawa et al, <citation rid="CR45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s0896-6273(01)00189-1" pmid="11182090" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>We expect that all LOF variants of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> will be tolerated in a heterozygous state and hence are rarely found in patients. <sentence_start/>This contrasts with <italic toggle="yes">CLCN4</italic> for which many pathogenic LOF variants were described (Palmer et al, <citation rid="CR35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/mp.2016.135" pmid="27550844" pmcid="PMC5794876" count="1">2018</citation>, <citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41380-022-01852-9" pmid="36385166" pmcid="PMC9908558" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>This is due to the X-chromosomal localization of human <italic toggle="yes">CLCN4:</italic> males have no WT allele, which might compensate for the LOF variant.

Based on these considerations, it is not surprising that the majority of <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants in our cohort likely cause a gain-of-function (GOF). <sentence_start/>Variants increasing ClC-3 ion exchange activity, either quantitatively or qualitatively (e.g., by broadening the voltage range over which ion transport occurs), may exert a dominant toxic effect in heterozygous individuals. <sentence_start/>Our previous work (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>), which ignored the effects of T9 subunits, suggested p.Ile607Thr as a GOF variant. <sentence_start/>It moderately increased ClC-3 current at neutral pH. <sentence_start/>More importantly, it enabled currents at more negative cytoplasmic voltages, suggesting that its ion transport may be overstimulated at physiological endosomal voltages. <sentence_start/>In the present cohort, we identified an additional missense variant affecting the same residue, p.Ile607Val, as well as multiple other variants located in different regions of the protein that produced similar biophysical alterations. <sentence_start/>Together, these variants point to a shared pathogenic mechanism.

The recent discovery of T9 proteins as inhibitory subunits for the ClC-3 to ClC-5 clade (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>) raised the question of whether these variants might be resistant to T9-mediated inhibition, a prerequisite for changes in voltage-dependence to have an effect. <sentence_start/>Whereas co-expression with T9A<sup>ΔpAC</sup>, which permits surface expression while retaining the inhibitory CID domain, suppressed these currents (Fig. 2E), the variants displayed sufficient resistance to inhibition to generate large vesicles in the vacuolization assay (Fig. 2F). <sentence_start/>This apparent discrepancy echoes earlier findings (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>) showing that disease-causing variants may entail partial resistance to T9 in ClC-3-based vacuolization assays, while not generating detectable PM currents. <sentence_start/>This suggests that even a small relief from T9 inhibition can cause vacuolization, although it is not sufficient to increase plasma membrane currents above background. <sentence_start/>The apparently higher sensitivity of the vacuolization assay may be owed to the integration of small increases in volume over time, or to differences in the membrane environment. <sentence_start/>Both types of assays only qualitatively reflect ion transport, as the human variants may also affect subcellular trafficking of the transporters. <sentence_start/>The weakened T9-mediated inhibition of this class of variants, which display significant inward currents, raises the question of whether their altered current rectification is required for vacuolization and pathogenicity. <sentence_start/>Supporting this idea, disease-causing variants in ClC-6 (Polovitskaya et al, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2020.11.004" pmid="33217309" pmcid="PMC7820737" count="1">2020</citation>; Zhang et al, <citation rid="CR54" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/sciadv.adg4479" pmid="37831762" pmcid="PMC10575590" count="1">2023</citation>) and ClC-7 (Nicoli et al, <citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2019.04.008" pmid="31155284" pmcid="PMC6562152" count="1">2019</citation>; Polovitskaya et al, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jbc.2024.107437" pmid="38838776" pmcid="PMC11261146" count="1">2024</citation>; Lee et al, <citation rid="CR25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/mgg3.2494" pmcid="PMC11273547" pmid="39056574" count="1">2024</citation>)-CLC exchangers without known inhibitory β-subunits-shift voltage dependence toward more negative voltages and cause vacuolization.

Another class of pathogenic <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants partially relieves T9-mediated inhibition without significantly changing PM currents in the absence of T9. <sentence_start/>The affected residues (Tyr<sup>85</sup>, Asp<sup>87</sup>, Ile<sup>252</sup>, His<sup>287</sup>, and Arg<sup>710</sup>) are located in a region previously shown to be important for binding the inhibitory carboxy-terminus (CID) of T9 proteins (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>; Schrecker et al, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-025-01617-2" pmcid="PMC12403049" pmid="40670814" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Underlining shared pathogenic mechanisms, the ClC-4 equivalent of ClC-3 Asp<sup>87</sup>-deleted in subject #6 and replaced by Val in subject #7-was changed to Glu in an individual carrying the <italic toggle="yes">CLCN4</italic> p.Asp29Glu variant, and the pathogenic <italic toggle="yes">CLCN4</italic> p.Arg652Thr variant affects the residue corresponding to Arg<sup>710</sup> in ClC-3 that is changed in the present <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> p.Arg710Gly variant (Palmer et al, <citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41380-022-01852-9" pmid="36385166" pmcid="PMC9908558" count="1">2023</citation>; Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>These variants display a clear quantitative gain of transport activity without altering the biophysical properties of ClC-3 currents.

One missense variant (p.Trp385Cys) was identified in the homozygous state, with both parents being unaffected. <sentence_start/>Bioinformatic analyses suggested this variant to be damaging (Dataset EV1). <sentence_start/>Functionally, it showed features suggestive of increased endosomal activity, including reduced inhibition by acidic pH; however, it did not induce vacuolization upon overexpression together with T9A. Although these subtle functional alterations may be amplified by homozygous expression in the proband, it remains unclear whether they are sufficient to account for the observed disease phenotype.

Eight missense variants found in NDD individuals (Dataset EV2) neither significantly changed plasma-membrane currents nor showed resistance to T9 inhibition in the vacuolization assay (Fig. EV2). <sentence_start/>Our functional assays therefore failed to support their pathogenicity. <sentence_start/>However, these variants are extremely rare in or absent from population databases, and we cannot rule out that they may cause defects not captured by our overexpression assays, such as altered subcellular localization in neurons or changes in regulatory mechanisms.

In our assays, GOF variants caused the formation of large lysosome-like compartments, likely due to H⁺-gradient-driven luminal Cl⁻ accumulation, followed by osmotic swelling and impaired vesicle scission (Polovitskaya et al, <citation rid="CR37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2020.11.004" pmid="33217309" pmcid="PMC7820737" count="1">2020</citation>). <sentence_start/>It remains unclear whether this effect occurs only upon overexpression in vitro or also in human subjects, as observed with strongly activating <italic toggle="yes">CLCN7</italic> variants associated with vacuolization in many tissues (HOD syndrome, OMIM: ) (Leray et al, <citation rid="CR27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.74136" pmid="35670560" pmcid="PMC9242644" count="1">2022</citation>; Nicoli et al, <citation rid="CR32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2019.04.008" pmid="31155284" pmcid="PMC6562152" count="1">2019</citation>; Polovitskaya et al, <citation rid="CR38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jbc.2024.107437" pmid="38838776" pmcid="PMC11261146" count="1">2024</citation>). <sentence_start/>The absence of organomegaly, a hallmark of HOD, argues against this possibility in the present subjects. <sentence_start/>The precise mechanisms by which <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants lead to disease remain unclear and may vary with the particular type of variant. <sentence_start/>The observation that both LOF and GOF variants in <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">CLCN4</italic> (Palmer et al, <citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41380-022-01852-9" pmid="36385166" pmcid="PMC9908558" count="1">2023</citation>; Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>) can produce similar symptoms suggests somewhat general effects, potentially including altered trafficking of neuronal receptors and channels (Qi et al, <citation rid="CR39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/brain/awaf243" pmcid="PMC12677024" pmid="40605603" count="1">2025</citation>).
Implication for the structure-function relationship of ClC-3/T9

Several newly identified variants affected residues that are located in the region of ClC-3 that binds T9’s inhibitory carboxyterminal domain (CID). <sentence_start/>These findings confirm and extend our previous analysis (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>; Schrecker et al, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-025-01617-2" pmcid="PMC12403049" pmid="40670814" count="1">2025</citation>) and provide a clear mechanism for a toxic GOF. <sentence_start/>Other variants affecting residues in different regions allowed inward currents at acidic pH, suggesting a gain of function. <sentence_start/>Intriguingly, all these variants also weakened T9-mediated inhibition in the vacuolization assay despite the fact that the altered residues are far from the CID-binding region. <sentence_start/>Hence, gating-associated conformational changes may change binding affinity. <sentence_start/>Notably, functional assays of disease-associated Arg<sup>710</sup> and Thr<sup>713</sup> variants (the equivalent residues of ClC-4 are found mutated in NDD (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>); and Fig. 3) suggest that CID interacts with the cytoplasmic CBS1 domain even though both residues are not in close proximity to CID in the state captured by cryo-EM (Schrecker et al, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-025-01617-2" pmcid="PMC12403049" pmid="40670814" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Cytoplasmic CBS domains of CLC proteins undergo substantial, poorly defined rearrangements during ‘common’ gating of CLCs (Bykova et al, <citation rid="CR3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nsmb1176" pmid="17115052" count="1">2006</citation>; Leisle et al, <citation rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.51224" pmid="32343228" pmcid="PMC7274781" count="1">2020</citation>; Hilton et al, <citation rid="CR17" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1101/2025.10.01.679551" count="1">2025</citation>) and hence might contact CID in a different conformational state. <sentence_start/>Intriguingly, alteration of residues involved in CID binding and T9-mediated inhibition (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>; Schrecker et al, <citation rid="CR42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41594-025-01617-2" pmcid="PMC12403049" pmid="40670814" count="1">2025</citation>), including the aforementioned Arg<sup>710</sup> of CBS1 or N-terminal Tyr<sup>85</sup> and Asp<sup>87</sup>, resulted in a slight increase of inward currents at acidic pH (Fig. 3A,B). <sentence_start/>Thus, modulation of T9 binding through gating-dependent conformational changes appears plausible.

The structural basis for CLC exchanger gating, which involves both subunits in a common process (Ludwig et al, <citation rid="CR29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1074/jbc.M113.509364" pmid="23983121" pmcid="PMC3789960" count="1">2013</citation>), remains poorly understood. <sentence_start/>The present work provides additional insights. <sentence_start/>ClC-3 Ile<sup>607</sup>, whose alteration to Thr (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>) or Val (this work) yields additional inward currents, resides at the interface between the two CLC monomers (Fig. 1B). <sentence_start/>In <italic toggle="yes">E.coli</italic> ecClC-1, replacing the equivalent Ile<sup>442</sup> with Trp resulted in a predominantly monomeric transporter (Robertson et al, <citation rid="CR55" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nature09556" pmcid="PMC3057488" pmid="21048711" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, since overall gating is conserved with p.Ile607Thr and p.Ile607Val substitutions, these variants are unlikely to impede dimerization. <sentence_start/>Instead, they may subtly change subunit interactions that are necessary for common gating. <sentence_start/>The other two residues associated with inward currents, Val<sup>324</sup> and Gly<sup>327</sup>, are located around the ‘external’ conserved Phe<sup>326</sup>, which interacts with the protonated E<sub>gate</sub> in the course of the transport cycle (Leisle et al, <citation rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.51224" pmid="32343228" pmcid="PMC7274781" count="1">2020</citation>) (Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>Changing this ‘gating glutamate’ affects common gating of CLC channels and transporters, protopore gating of ClC-0, and exchange stoichiometry (Leisle et al, <citation rid="CR26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.51224" pmid="32343228" pmcid="PMC7274781" count="1">2020</citation>; Palmer et al, <citation rid="CR34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41380-022-01852-9" pmid="36385166" pmcid="PMC9908558" count="1">2023</citation>). <sentence_start/>It is conceivable that changes in the neighboring residues may perturb the movement of E<sub>gate</sub> in the course of common gating.

Although the present cohort, which includes previously reported individuals (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>), is the largest published to date, it remains difficult to establish clear correlations between specific variants and clinical phenotypes. <sentence_start/>Only a general picture emerges: Homozygous LOF variants are associated with earlier onset and more severe symptoms compared to the heterozygous GOF variants. <sentence_start/>This included neonatal onset hypotonia and nystagmus, with seizures beginning at a mean age of 4 months and initially presenting as focal-onset seizures, epileptic spasms, or hypermotor seizures. <sentence_start/>Motor outcomes included bilateral spastic cerebral palsy in one subject, while dystonia was absent. <sentence_start/>Subjects with heterozygous GOF variants showed later developmental concerns (mean 7.7 months), no neonatal nystagmus, and later-onset seizures (mean 2.9 years), initially manifesting as generalized seizures such as absence seizures. <sentence_start/>Movement abnormalities included dystonia in three individuals, whereas bilateral spastic cerebral palsy was not observed.
Conclusion

In conclusion, we report sixteen individuals with neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and function-changing <italic toggle="yes">CLCN3</italic> variants, of which six were previously reported: two with biallelic LOF variants, thirteen with heterozygous GOF variants, and one with a biallelic variant of unclear functional consequences. <sentence_start/>Although this is the largest known dataset, the sample size still limits the ability to establish robust genotype-phenotype correlations or to draw definitive conclusions regarding variant-specific clinical trajectories. <sentence_start/>In contrast to the previous studies (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>; Nakashima et al, <citation rid="CR30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s10038-022-01106-0" pmid="36536096" pmcid="PMC12327483" count="1">2023</citation>), our functional analysis systematically addressed the effects of recently identified inhibitory T9 β-subunits (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Although relying on overexpression in mammalian cells and neglecting the effects of ClC-4 with which ClC-3 heteromerizes in the brain (Weinert et al, <citation rid="CR50" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.15252/embj.2019103358" pmid="32118314" pmcid="PMC7196918" count="1">2020</citation>; Balduin et al, <citation rid="CR2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-025-19757-2" pmid="41023377" pmcid="PMC12479943" count="1">2025</citation>), our results revealed that ~2/3 of ClC-3 missense variants identified in subjects with NDD exhibit a gain of ion transport. <sentence_start/>These variants fell into two groups: those that reduce T9-mediated inhibition by altering residues within the binding region for its C-terminal inhibitory domain, and those changing ClC-3 gating, enabling currents across a broader voltage range. <sentence_start/>Notably, gating-altering variants also attenuated T9 inhibition, revealing a previously unrecognized link between gating-associated conformational changes and CID-binding affinity. <sentence_start/>Our findings advance clinical interpretation and mechanistic understanding of CLC/T9 ion exchangers.
Methods
Study cohort

Subjects were identified through GeneMatcher (Sobreira et al, <citation rid="CR44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/humu.22844" pmid="26220891" pmcid="PMC4833888" count="1">2015</citation>), ERN-ITHACA-a European Rare Disease Network for rare congenital malformations and intellectual disability, ERN EpiCARE-a European rare-disease network of Epilepsy and Genetics departments, or by being contacted as the corresponding author of a previous publication (Duncan et al, <citation rid="CR9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.ajhg.2021.06.003" pmid="34186028" pmcid="PMC8387284" count="1">2021</citation>). <sentence_start/>We also contacted authors of previous publications and asked for updates on published subjects. <sentence_start/>Clinical and genetic data were collected using standardized forms completed by clinicians or caregivers. <sentence_start/>Collected variables included developmental milestones, cognition and behavior, seizure and movement disorder history (including age of onset and offset and seizure semiology), developmental trajectory, physical examination findings, and results of electroencephalography and neuroimaging. <sentence_start/>The study was approved by the local ethics committees. <sentence_start/>The study complies with the principles laid out in the Declaration of Helsinki. <sentence_start/>As all probands were minors or had cognitive impairment, their parents or legal guardians provided written informed consent.

Expression constructs and cell culture

Mouse ClC-3 splice variant c and human ClC-3 splice variant a cDNAs were inserted into a modified pEGFP-C1 (Clontech) vector, where EGFP was replaced by mVenus. <sentence_start/>Untagged T9A cDNA was cloned into pCDNA3.1 (Thermo Fisher) (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>Untagged CD4 was used as a transfection control. <sentence_start/>Missense variants were introduced using the QuikChange approach (Agilent), mutagenesis primers are listed in Table EV1. <sentence_start/>All clones were verified by Sanger sequencing the entire ORF.

WT HeLa and <italic toggle="yes">TMEM206</italic><sup>−/−</sup> HEK293 cells (Ullrich et al, <citation rid="CR47" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7554/eLife.49187" pmid="31318332" pmcid="PMC6663466" count="1">2019</citation>) were maintained in DMEM with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin at 37 °C and 5% CO<sub>2</sub>. <sentence_start/>Cells were transfected 48 h before experiments using Lipofectamine 2000 (Thermo Fisher) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Immunocytochemistry

Immunofluorescent staining was performed as described in (Planells-Cases et al, <citation rid="CR36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41467-025-58546-3" pmid="40169677" pmcid="PMC11962092" count="1">2025</citation>). <sentence_start/>WT HeLa cells were seeded on uncoated glass coverslips 2 h prior to transfection and co-transfected with Venus-ClC-3a (WT or mutants) plus untagged T9A, or CD4 as a control, at 1:1 DNA ratio. <sentence_start/>48 h post transfection, cells were fixed with methanol in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 10 min, permeabilized with 0.1% saponin and blocked in 3% goat serum, 2% BSA in PBS and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies (listed in Reagents and Tools Table) in 0.05% saponin, 3% BSA in PBS. <sentence_start/>Subsequently, cells were incubated for 1-2 h at room temperature with secondary antibodies coupled to fluorophores (listed in Reagents and Tools Table) and DAPI, washed thrice with PBS, and mounted on slides with Fluoromount-G™. <sentence_start/>Slides were imaged with the LSM880 confocal microscope with a ×63, 1.4 numerical aperture oil-immersion lens (Zeiss). <sentence_start/>The experiment was performed in a non-blinded manner, at least in three transfections, with at least ten images taken per slide.
Lysosensor staining

WT HeLa cells were seeded onto glass-bottom MatTek imaging dishes 2 h prior to transfection and co-transfected with Venus-ClC-3a (WT or mutants) plus untagged T9A, or CD4 as a control, at 1:1 DNA ratio. <sentence_start/>After 48 h, cells were incubated for 15 min at 37 °C with 5 μM Lysosensor®Yellow/Blue DND-160 (Invitrogen, #L7545) in complete DMEM medium, washed twice with prewarmed PBS and immediately imaged in HBSS medium for the following 15 min. <sentence_start/>Cells were imaged at the LSM880 confocal microscope (Zeiss) at ×63 magnification using <italic toggle="yes">λ</italic><sub>ex</sub> = 405 nm and <italic toggle="yes">λ</italic><sub>em</sub> = 511-588 nm for Lysosensor®, and <italic toggle="yes">λ</italic><sub>ex</sub> = 488 nm for Venus. <sentence_start/>Experiments were performed in a non-blinded manner at least in three independent transfections with 4−9 images taken from each dish.

Vesicle area was quantified from the Lysosensor® (blue) channel using a custom Python (Python Software Foundation) script. <sentence_start/>Putative vesicle locations were identified using a multi-scale Laplacian-of-Gaussian (LoG) blob detector applied to a lightly contrast-enhanced image (contrast-limited adaptive histogram equalization, CLAHE) followed by mild Gaussian smoothing to reduce pixel noise. <sentence_start/>Candidate vesicle centers were defined as local maxima in the LoG response across spatial scales, enabling detection of vesicles across a range of sizes.

To obtain the total vesicle area around a candidate center, a small image patch around the center was extracted and threshold-based segmentation was performed on a Gaussian-smoothed version of the raw (non-contrast-enhanced) image. <sentence_start/>The threshold was selected by combining Otsu thresholding with constraints based on the center intensity and local background, so that the candidate center remained within the segmented foreground. <sentence_start/>When multiple contiguous regions were present within the patch, only the region containing the center was retained as the vesicle lumen. <sentence_start/>In crowded regions where a single segmented region could include more than one vesicle connected with a narrow neck, touching objects could be separated using a distance-transform watershed approach. <sentence_start/>Very large, approximately round lumen-positive structures were summarized by fitting a circle to outline points. <sentence_start/>Duplicate detections were suppressed using non-maximum suppression based on center proximity and overlap (intersection-over-union criteria), and small detections fully contained within larger vesicles were removed. <sentence_start/>To improve performance in bright and densely populated regions, detection was run in two passes by masking objects above a user-defined size cutoff after the first pass with masked pixels replaced by a local background estimate to avoid introducing sharp edges, followed by pooling detections and final de-duplication. <sentence_start/>For each detected object, relative standard deviation of the intensity was calculated and top 1% of detection were flagged for each image as possible false-positives. <sentence_start/>For each detected object, area, area-equivalent radius and intensity summary statistics were exported, and overlays of detected objects were visualized for quality control (Fig. EV3).Figure EV3

Vesicle area data are presented as probability density distributions, with control measurements taken from matched WT samples imaged in the same experimental sessions as the corresponding mutant. <sentence_start/>Because the analysis workflow does not include cell segmentation or gating by transfection status, vesicles from both transfected and non-transfected cells contribute to each distribution; this is expected to dilute variant-associated shifts and may therefore underestimate the magnitude of variants’ effects.
Electrophysiology

For patch-clamp recordings, cells transfected 48 h earlier were seeded on poly-L-lysine-coated (Sigma-Aldrich, P4707) coverslips 1-5 h before measurement. <sentence_start/>Whole-cell patch-clamp experiments were performed using an EPC-10 USB patch-clamp amplifier and PATCHMASTER software (HEKA Elektronik). <sentence_start/>Currents were sampled at 20 kHz and low-pass filtered at 2 kHz. <sentence_start/>Patch pipettes had a resistance of 3-5 MΩ. <sentence_start/>The series resistance did not exceed 10 MΩ and was compensated by at least 30%. <sentence_start/>Voltage step protocol consisted of 100-ms test voltage steps at −120 mV to +160 mV in 20 mV increments from the holding potential of −30 mV. <sentence_start/>Voltage steps were followed by a 100-ms step at −80 mV and applied at 2 s intervals. <sentence_start/>Currents were normalized to cell capacitance to yield current density.

The patch pipette solution contained in mM: 140 CsCl, 5 EGTA, 1 MgCl<sub>2</sub>, 10 HEPES, with pH adjusted to 7.2 with CsOH (275 mOsm/kg). <sentence_start/>Standard bath solution contained (in mM): 150 NaCl, 6 CsCl, 1 MgCl<sub>2</sub>, 1.5 CaCl<sub>2</sub>, 10 D-glucose, 10 HEPES (pH adjusted to 7.5 using NaOH) (320 mOsm/kg). <sentence_start/>For bath pH 4.5, HEPES was substituted with 5 mM citrate/citric acid buffer.
Data was analyzed using the SciPy 1.5.2 library for Python 3.8 programming language (Python Software Foundation).
